name: Mayer-Rokitansky-Kuster-Hauser syndrome
aliases: congenital absence of the uterus and vagina

reference.source: Standard gynaecology texts / international guidance on mullerian anomalies
clinicalPearls: MRKH is congenital agenesis or hypoplasia of the uterus and upper vagina from failure of mullerian duct development in a genetically and phenotypically female individual
It typically presents as primary amenorrhoea with normal secondary sexual characteristics and normal female external genitalia
The karyotype is 46,XX and the ovaries are present and functional, so pubertal development and hormone production are normal
The vagina is short or absent, which may also present as difficulty with intercourse
The type 1 form is isolated to the reproductive tract, while type 2 is associated with renal, skeletal, and other anomalies
Renal anomalies such as a solitary, pelvic, or absent kidney and vertebral or other skeletal defects are important associations to screen for
Management combines psychological support with creation of a functional vagina, using vaginal dilation as first-line and surgery when needed
Because the ovaries are normal, biological parenthood may be possible through assisted reproduction with a gestational carrier
reference.pathophysiology: Mayer-Rokitansky-Kuster-Hauser syndrome results from failure of development of the mullerian (paramesonephric) ducts, which normally form the uterus, cervix, and upper vagina. The defect leaves absent or rudimentary uterine structures and a shortened or absent upper vagina, while the lower vagina, derived separately, and the external genitalia are normal. Because ovarian tissue arises independently and is unaffected, the ovaries function normally with a 46,XX karyotype, producing normal secondary sexual characteristics. Shared embryological timing with the developing urinary and axial skeletal systems explains the frequent association with renal and vertebral anomalies in the type 2 form.
additionalDifferentials: Transverse vaginal septum or imperforate hymen with outflow obstruction
Isolated vaginal agenesis with a functioning uterus
Other causes of primary amenorrhoea including hypothalamic and pituitary disorders
additionalInvestigations: Pelvic ultrasound to assess uterus, vagina, and ovaries
Pelvic magnetic resonance imaging to define mullerian and any rudimentary uterine structures
Karyotype to confirm 46,XX and distinguish from androgen insensitivity
Serum hormone profile confirming normal ovarian function
Renal tract imaging to detect associated urinary anomalies
Spinal and skeletal imaging where indicated for associated anomalies
redFlags: Cyclical pelvic pain suggesting a functioning rudimentary uterine horn with obstructed menstruation
Undiagnosed associated renal anomaly affecting overall health
Significant psychological distress requiring dedicated support
Diagnostic uncertainty needing distinction from androgen insensitivity or a disorder of sex development
reference.prognosis: MRKH does not affect general health or life expectancy, and normal ovarian function preserves endocrine health and the potential for genetic offspring through assisted reproduction with a surrogate. With dilation or surgery a functional vagina can usually be achieved, and psychological support is central to long-term wellbeing.
pitfalls: Confusing MRKH with androgen insensitivity by not checking karyotype and hormone profile
Failing to screen for associated renal and skeletal anomalies
Missing a functioning rudimentary uterine horn causing cyclical obstructed pain
Neglecting the psychological impact and support needs of the diagnosis
references: International consensus and ESHRE/ESGE classification of female genital anomalies
Guidance on management of mullerian agenesis
management: Graduated vaginal dilation therapy as first-line creation of a functional vagina
Vaginoplasty (skin-graft, bowel or traction techniques) when dilation is unsuccessful or not chosen
Psychological support and counselling around the diagnosis, sexual function and future fertility
Assisted reproduction using the woman's own oocytes with a gestational carrier, or uterus transplantation where available
Screen for and manage associated renal tract, vertebral and skeletal anomalies with appropriate imaging and specialist referral
Coordinated multidisciplinary care and long-term follow-up through gynaecology, urology and psychology
Genetic counselling for the individual and family given occasional familial clustering
